Scottish dance band (N3)

Vamp (N4)

A vamp accompaniment can be played on piano, accordion or guitar.
Folk group (N3)
A group of singers and instrumentalists who perform traditional music from a particular country, e.g. Scotland and Ireland. 
Scottish folk music instruments might include fiddle, whistle, guitar, accordion and singers.

evidence.supportingText:
Baroque (N4)
The Baroque period in music, art, architecture, and fashion was fancy, highly detailed and ornamented. 
Harpsichord (N4)
The harpsichord was a popular keyboard instrument in the Baroque period, with its distinctive plucked sound.
Organ (N3)
Another popular keyboard instrument in baroque music is the pipe organ. In some pieces you may hear an organ playing along with the strings instead of the harpsichord.
Recorder (N4)
The recorder is a woodwind instrument which was popular in the Baroque period and came in many different sizes. 
The strings were very important in the Baroque period. The other sections of the orchestra had not yet become fully established.

Trill (N5)

A grace note is another ornament you’ve already learned about.

evidence.supportingText: Music from approximately 1810-1900, following the Classical period. Common features include expressive melody, rubato, chromatic harmony, wide dynamic range, programmatic ideas and an expanded orchestra. evidence.supportingText:
Romantic (N4)
The Romantic period in music, art, literature and fashion focused on free emotional expression. The individual imagination was seen as more important than the Classical ideas of form, structure and balance.
The orchestra became much larger in the Romantic period, with the addition of more woodwind, brass and percussion, and an increase in the numbers of string players. This resulted in huge and powerful orchestral works.
Romantic composers moved away from Classical musical formulas in order to express greater emotion in their music. As a result, Romantic music usually has: 
Expression and emotion 
A large orchestra  
A wide dynamic range 
A rubato tempo
A chromatic melody   
Rubato (N5)
Rubato is when the performer can have a bit of freedom with the speed of the music by speeding up and slowing down to add expression to the music.
Chromatic (N5)
Use of the chromatic scale was quite common in Romantic music. This is when composers would use notes outside the key signature.

evidence.supportingText:
Chamber music (H) instrumental style
Chamber music is music written to be performed by a small group of musicians, in a small room rather than in a big hall. 
In a chamber ensemble only one musician plays each part. 
Common chamber music ensembles include trios, quartets, quintets and octets.
These are usually made up of related instruments e.g. a wind quintet of flute, oboe, clarinet, French horn and bassoon.
String quartet (H) instrumental style
A string quartet is a chamber ensemble, containing two violins, one viola and one cello.

evidence.supportingText:
Impressionist (H) instrumental style
The term impressionist is borrowed from a style of painting in which the images were blurred and hazy. 
20th Century composers attempted to incorporate the same vague, hazy feelings into their music.

Composers ‘broke the rules’ to increase and develop a pallet of tonal colours, like a painter.

evidence.supportingText:
Lied (H) vocal style

evidence.supportingText:
Both minor scales usually emote serious, sad or angry feelings. The harmonic minor scale has a distinctive sound due to this interval:
3 semitones3 semitones
3 semitones
3 semitones
Melodic minor scale (H)
Some composers felt the 3-semitone leap in the harmonic minor scale to be awkward, particularly in vocal music. To eliminate this, these composers either sharpened the 6th degree or flattened the 7th by a semitone.
The melodic minor scale is formed by using both solutions. The sharpened 6th appears in the ascending form of the scale, while the flattened 7th appears in the descending form of the scale.

evidence.supportingText:
Nationalist Romantic Period
Nationalist (AH)  
Music that expresses a strong connection with a composer's country or national identity. Nationalist ideas became especially significant during the 19th century.
•  Folk tunes, songs or traditional dance rhythms.
•  Stories, legends, historical events or national heroes.
•  Landscapes and places associated with the composer's country.
•  Distinctive instruments, scales, rhythms or styles associated with a culture.
Sibelius: Finlandia
Jean Sibelius, a Romantic-period Finnish composer, played an important role in the formation of Finnish national identity. His symphonic poem Finlandia was composed in response to censorship imposed by the Russian Empire. Its rousing, turbulent music came to symbolise the Finnish national struggle.
Opening sound
Low brass, timpani and growling discords create a sinister, menacing atmosphere.
This may suggest oppression or conflict; explain interpretations as possibilities rather than fixed facts.

evidence.supportingText: Music organised by a predetermined series rather than traditional functional tonality. evidence.supportingText:
Serial music tone rows
Serial (AH)  A style of composition based on an ordered series of musical elements. Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes of the chromatic scale are organised into a tone row before any note is repeated.
Tone row or note row (AH)  The fixed order of pitches used as the source of the work’s melodies and harmonies.
Row form
Meaning
Original
The row in its starting form.
Retrograde
The row played in reverse order.
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.

evidence.supportingText:
Serial music tone rows
Serial (AH)  A style of composition based on an ordered series of musical elements. Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes of the chromatic scale are organised into a tone row before any note is repeated.
Tone row or note row (AH)  The fixed order of pitches used as the source of the work’s melodies and harmonies.
Row form
Meaning
Original
The row in its starting form.
Retrograde
The row played in reverse order.
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.
Tone-row activity compose and transform
•  1. Create a four-note row — choose four different notes and place them in an order.
•  2. Add a rhythm — give the four notes a clear rhythmic pattern.
•  3. Create the retrograde — write or play the notes in reverse order.
•  4. Create the inversion — reverse the direction of every interval.
•  5. Combine ideas — perform in pairs using different rhythms, retrograde and transposition.

Leitmotif (AH)  
A short recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, object, place, emotion or plot element.
Wagner used leitmotifs to help organise long dramatic works and connect music with the story.

•  Places — for example a river, home or landscape.
•  Emotions or ideas — for example love, destiny or death.

Listen for a recognisable melodic shape even when the orchestration has changed.

evidence.supportingText:
Sprechgesang vocal technique
Sprechgesang (AH)  A vocal technique in which the performer uses the voice expressively, halfway between speaking and singing. The text is recited on indicated pitches rather than sung conventionally.
The word
Sprech — speech or speaking
Gesang — song or singing
Composers including Arnold Schoenberg and Alban Berg used the technique; many well-known examples therefore use German texts.
Listen to Mondestrunken from Schoenberg’s Pierrot Lunaire. The work is atonal and the performer is sometimes dressed as Pierrot, the clown-like character at the centre of the cycle.
Important: Sprechgesang is a vocal technique, not a style of music.

decisions: User accepted pilot approach and requested every level plus a Hub Listening review tile on 2026-11-06.
AH Subject stays fugue-specific; Higher Subject points to the same fact.
Cross-level alternatives sharing one fact have variantOfQuestionId; they count once in distinctFactGroups.
One extra bagpipe/drone paraphrase removed; retired question ID CQ-N3-MC0044-02 is not reused.
Chord question avoids the overbroad three-note-chord equals triad source claim.
Bowed question does not require later-level Arco vocabulary.
Reviewed content and uncertain examples remain for teacher review. No audio or extended exam-style practice was generated.
Latest request supersedes earlier exclusions and shared-only coverage: every current Dictionary concept has at least three own questions.
Higher Subject now uses sonata-form context; Advanced Higher Subject remains fugue-specific.
Scenario alternatives share fact groups and are not counted as separate facts.
Approval statuses were removed; all valid questions are available for quizzes.
verificationLimits: Exact local source matches and structural/editorial checks are not comprehensive independent verification of every musical claim.
Historical and style examples carry the Dictionary context; uncertain absolutes have been qualified or omitted.
No recording was auditioned or approved.

Supplied workbook coverage is incomplete for AH chord II/first inversion and the minor-key extension of AH I/IV/V/VI progressions. Named instrument listening exercises do not spell out every sound adjective; those remain Dictionary-supported. No audio excerpts are attached or auditioned in this text-question audit.
authoringNotes: Every N3/N4 concept has three draft candidates; no exclusions or shared-only rows remain.
First eight N3 style sets are rewritten: no impossible distractors, history-only date questions or exclusive identification of broad genres from generic clues.
N4 Octave explicitly shares the N3 octave fact group while retaining three actual question records.
Local Dictionary contains a potentially overbroad every-three-note-chord-is-triad claim and inconsistent off-beat/backbeat wording. New questions avoid those claims.

Romantic (N4)
The Romantic period in music, art, literature and fashion focused on free emotional expression. The individual imagination was seen as more important than the Classical ideas of form, structure and balance.
The orchestra became much larger in the Romantic period, with the addition of more woodwind, brass and percussion, and an increase in the numbers of string players. This resulted in huge and powerful orchestral works.
Romantic composers moved away from Classical musical formulas in order to express greater emotion in their music. As a result, Romantic music usually has: 
Expression and emotion 
A large orchestra  
A wide dynamic range 
A rubato tempo
A chromatic melody   
Rubato (N5)
Rubato is when the performer can have a bit of freedom with the speed of the music by speeding up and slowing down to add expression to the music.
Chromatic (N5)
Use of the chromatic scale was quite common in Romantic music. This is when composers would use notes outside the key signature.

Different music for each verse, no repetition.

Melodic minor scale (H)
Some composers felt the 3-semitone leap in the harmonic minor scale to be awkward, particularly in vocal music. To eliminate this, these composers either sharpened the 6th degree or flattened the 7th by a semitone.

•  Experimental instrumental effects, such as melodic instruments used percussively and harmonics.
•  Unconventional jazz instruments, including flugelhorn, flute and oboe.

evidence.supportingText:
Serial music tone rows
Serial (AH)  A style of composition based on an ordered series of musical elements. Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes of the chromatic scale are organised into a tone row before any note is repeated.
Tone row or note row (AH)  The fixed order of pitches used as the source of the work’s melodies and harmonies.
Row form
Meaning
Original
The row in its starting form.
Retrograde
The row played in reverse order.
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.

Polytonality or bitonality tonality
Polytonality (AH)  The simultaneous use of music in more than one key. Bitonality is the simultaneous use of two keys.

Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.

The inverted row played in reverse order.

Tone-row activity compose and transform
•  1. Create a four-note row — choose four different notes and place them in an order.
•  2. Add a rhythm — give the four notes a clear rhythmic pattern.
•  3. Create the retrograde — write or play the notes in reverse order.
•  4. Create the inversion — reverse the direction of every interval.
•  5. Combine ideas — perform in pairs using different rhythms, retrograde and transposition.

evidence.supportingText:
Leitmotif Romantic Period
Leitmotif (AH)  
A short recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, object, place, emotion or plot element.
Wagner used leitmotifs to help organise long dramatic works and connect music with the story.
•  Characters — for example a hero or other named figure.
•  Objects — for example a ring or sword.
•  Places — for example a river, home or landscape.
•  Emotions or ideas — for example love, destiny or death.
How leitmotifs change
A leitmotif may return in different keys, tempos, dynamics, rhythms or timbres to reflect the changing mood or action.
Listen for a recognisable melodic shape even when the orchestration has changed.

evidence.supportingText:
Sprechgesang vocal technique
Sprechgesang (AH)  A vocal technique in which the performer uses the voice expressively, halfway between speaking and singing. The text is recited on indicated pitches rather than sung conventionally.
The word
Sprech — speech or speaking
Gesang — song or singing
Composers including Arnold Schoenberg and Alban Berg used the technique; many well-known examples therefore use German texts.
Listen to Mondestrunken from Schoenberg’s Pierrot Lunaire. The work is atonal and the performer is sometimes dressed as Pierrot, the clown-like character at the centre of the cycle.
Important: Sprechgesang is a vocal technique, not a style of music.

Retrograde
The row played in reverse order.
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.
Tone-row activity compose and transform
•  1. Create a four-note row — choose four different notes and place them in an order.
•  2. Add a rhythm — give the four notes a clear rhythmic pattern.
•  3. Create the retrograde — write or play the notes in reverse order.
•  4. Create the inversion — reverse the direction of every interval.
•  5. Combine ideas — perform in pairs using different rhythms, retrograde and transposition.

evidence.supportingText:
Serial music tone rows
Serial (AH)  A style of composition based on an ordered series of musical elements. Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone method, in which all twelve notes of the chromatic scale are organised into a tone row before any note is repeated.
Tone row or note row (AH)  The fixed order of pitches used as the source of the work’s melodies and harmonies.
Row form
Meaning
Original
The row in its starting form.
Retrograde
The row played in reverse order.
Inversion
Each interval changes direction: up becomes down and down becomes up.
Retrograde inversion
The inverted row played in reverse order.
All melodic and harmonic material may be derived from the row. The result is often dissonant and atonal.
Tone-row activity compose and transform
•  1. Create a four-note row — choose four different notes and place them in an order.
•  2. Add a rhythm — give the four notes a clear rhythmic pattern.
•  3. Create the retrograde — write or play the notes in reverse order.
•  4. Create the inversion — reverse the direction of every interval.
•  5. Combine ideas — perform in pairs using different rhythms, retrograde and transposition.

A rhythmic device often at cadence points where accents shift to create the impression of a time change.

Leitmotif Romantic Period
Leitmotif (AH)  
A short recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, object, place, emotion or plot element.
Wagner used leitmotifs to help organise long dramatic works and connect music with the story.
•  Characters — for example a hero or other named figure.
•  Objects — for example a ring or sword.
•  Places — for example a river, home or landscape.
•  Emotions or ideas — for example love, destiny or death.
How leitmotifs change
A leitmotif may return in different keys, tempos, dynamics, rhythms or timbres to reflect the changing mood or action.
Listen for a recognisable melodic shape even when the orchestration has changed.

Sprechgesang vocal technique
Sprechgesang (AH)  A vocal technique in which the performer uses the voice expressively, halfway between speaking and singing. The text is recited on indicated pitches rather than sung conventionally.
The word
Sprech — speech or speaking
Gesang — song or singing
Composers including Arnold Schoenberg and Alban Berg used the technique; many well-known examples therefore use German texts.
Listen to Mondestrunken from Schoenberg’s Pierrot Lunaire. The work is atonal and the performer is sometimes dressed as Pierrot, the clown-like character at the centre of the cycle.
Important: Sprechgesang is a vocal technique, not a style of music.
